source.title: Nanomedicine, Volume I — Table 3-1: Elemental composition of the human body
source.author: Robert A. Freitas Jr.
source.note: Mass fractions are the measured quantity and are stored here as given; atom-count fractions are DERIVED in the figure from mass ÷ atomic weight, so the two orderings cannot disagree. Composition varies by a few per cent between individuals — chiefly with body fat and hydration — so these are representative, not exact. Origins follow Johnson 2019.

units.massPercent: per cent of total body mass

rows.name: Oxygen
rows.where: Mostly in water. Forged by fusion in massive stars and released when they explode.

rows.name: Carbon
rows.where: The backbone of every organic molecule in you. Made by helium fusion, mostly in dying low-mass stars.

rows.name: Hydrogen
rows.where: Made in the first microsecond. No star has ever made a hydrogen nucleus — stars destroy them.

rows.name: Nitrogen
rows.where: In every amino acid. Returned by the CNO cycle in dying stars, though the split between low-mass and massive sources is still argued about.

rows.name: Calcium
rows.where: Bone and teeth, and the signal that fires every one of your neurons.

rows.name: Phosphorus
rows.where: The backbone of DNA, and the energy currency of every cell.

rows.name: Potassium
rows.where: Nerve conduction. A small fraction is potassium-40, which is radioactive — you are very slightly so.

rows.name: Sulphur
rows.where: The cross-links that hold protein structures in shape.

rows.name: Sodium
rows.where: The other half of every nerve impulse.

rows.name: Chlorine
rows.where: Stomach acid, and the balance of fluid inside and outside your cells.

rows.name: Magnesium
rows.where: Sits at the centre of hundreds of enzymes.

rows.name: Iron
rows.where: Four grams. It carries every breath you take, and it sits at the exact point where fusion stops paying.
